caption:
Why do so many people feel less bloated or lose weight eating pasta in Italy? It’s probably not just one thing.

1. Traditional sauces are often simple. Many Italian sauces use just a handful of fresh ingredients like tomatoes, olive oil, basil, garlic, and Parmesan instead of heavy cream sauces or long ingredient lists. They’re often less calorie-dense, and you can absolutely make the same sauces at home.

2. Traditional durum wheat semolina pasta. Most dried Italian pasta is made from 100% durum wheat semolina, and it still contains gluten. What makes it different is its dense protein-starch structure, especially when cooked al dente, which slows digestion and helps keep you fuller longer. Some researchers think this may also mean less carbohydrate reaches the colon quickly, which could reduce fermentation and bloating in some people, although that hasn’t been definitively proven. The good news is that brands made with 100% durum semolina are widely available in U.S. grocery stores.

3. Smaller portions. Traditional pasta servings are often much smaller than what many restaurants serve elsewhere.

4. Slower, more intentional eating. Meals are meant to be enjoyed, giving your body more time to recognize fullness before you overeat.

5. More walking and less driving. On vacation you’re usually walking thousands of extra steps, climbing stairs, and moving throughout the day instead of driving everywhere. That extra activity adds up and supports digestion and energy balance.

6. Less stress and more relaxation. Vacations often mean lower stress, better sleep, and more time to enjoy meals, all of which can influence digestion.

The takeaway: You don’t have to move to Italy. You can recreate many of these habits at home—choose 100% durum wheat semolina pasta, cook it al dente, make simple sauces, eat reasonable portions, slow down during meals, and build more walking into your day.

Why does your menstrual cycle make you poop more? 

If your bowel habits completely change around your menstrual cycle, there’s actually a reason for it.

During menstruation, your body produces higher levels of prostaglandins. These chemicals help your uterus contract, but they don’t only affect the uterus—they can also stimulate your intestines.

When your colon contracts more, stool moves through your digestive tract faster. That means less water is absorbed, which can lead to loose stools, diarrhea, urgency, or going to the bathroom more often.

• Sip peppermint tea to help relax the muscles of the digestive tract.

• Fennel tea may help with menstrual discomfort and cramping.

• Ginger tea has been shown in studies to reduce menstrual cramps and may also help settle your stomach.

• Eat more soluble fiber, including oats, psyllium husk, and chia seeds. Soluble fiber absorbs water and can help improve stool consistency.

• Consider cutting back on caffeine if it tends to make your symptoms worse.

• Make sure you’re getting enough calcium-rich foods, including dairy or fortified non-dairy alternatives. Adequate calcium intake has been linked to fewer menstrual symptoms.

• Diets that are lower in fat and higher in vegetarian or plant-based foods have also been associated with less painful periods in some studies.

Period poops are incredibly common, and for most people they’re simply a normal response to hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle.

How I try to avoid food poisoning when I travel ✈️

A few simple habits can lower your risk:

• Wash your hands before you eat. It sounds simple, but germs from stool can easily spread to your hands from bathroom surfaces, door handles, phones, and other frequently touched objects.

• Choose foods that are freshly cooked and served hot. This is especially important in airports, food courts, and buffets.

• Avoid foods that have been sitting out at room temperature, especially meat, seafood, dairy products, rice, and sauces.

One thing many people don’t know is that bismuth subsalicylate has been shown in studies to reduce the risk of travelers’ diarrhea and is included as an option in travel medicine guidelines for some travelers.

However, bismuth is not appropriate for everyone. It can interact with certain medications, including blood thinners, aspirin, and other medications, and may not be safe for people with certain medical conditions. Be sure to discuss it with your healthcare professional before taking it.

Even if you do everything right, food poisoning and travelers’ diarrhea can still happen. But practicing good hand hygiene, choosing freshly cooked foods, and following food safety recommendations can significantly lower your risk while traveling.

This is not medical advice. This post is a review of gastroenterology and travel medicine guidelines for educational purposes only. Always discuss medications with your own healthcare professional before taking them.

caption:
Take it from two medical doctors and gut health experts: protein and fibre are not competing with each other biologically. 

They do entirely different jobs.

Protein is primarily absorbed in the small intestine, where it’s broken down into amino acids used to build muscle, enzymes, hormones and immune cells. Fibre largely bypasses that process altogether.

Your body can’t digest most fibre, which is exactly why it’s so important. Instead, it travels down to the colon where trillions of gut microbes ferment it into compounds that help maintain your gut lining, regulate inflammation, influence appetite, and even communicate with your brain.

If you eat large amounts of protein without enough fibre, some of that excess protein reaches the colon instead. Your microbes then ferment the protein rather than fibre, producing compounds like ammonia and hydrogen sulphide, which may negatively affect the gut environment over time.

This is one reason why the healthiest long-term dietary patterns consistently include both adequate protein and plenty of diverse plant fibre. Protein for your human cells, and fibre for the trillions of microbial cells that live alongside them.

How to Make Probiotic Pickles at Home 👇 

Use a fermentation crock or an airlock jar for best results. A regular mason jar also works, but if you use a standard lid you must loosen it daily to release gas (or it can explode, really).

You need:
•	2 lbs pickling cucumbers, ideally Kirby cucumbers.
•	4 cups filtered or dechlorinated water.
•	About 2 tbsp non-iodized salt per 4 cups water, or enough to make a roughly 3.5% brine.
•	4–6 garlic cloves, crushed.
•	Fresh dill or 1 tsp dill seed.
•	1 tsp mustard seed.
•	1 tsp whole peppercorns.
•	Red pepper flakes, optional.
•	1 grape leaf, or another tannin source if you want extra crunch.

Steps:
1.	Trim a thin slice from the blossom end of each cucumber.
2.	Dissolve the salt in room-temperature water until fully mixed.
3.	Put garlic, dill, and spices in the jar first, then pack in the cucumbers tightly. Leave about 1 inch of headspace.
4.	Pour in brine until the cucumbers are fully submerged. Weight them down if needed so none float above the brine.
5.	Cover with an airlock lid, or use a regular lid and burp daily.
6.	Ferment at room temperature until sour to taste, usually about 5–14 days depending on temperature and preference.
7.	Move to the refrigerator once they taste right. Keep the pickles submerged in brine and tightly covered.

The cyclospora outbreak has spawned a lot of bad advice. As a gastroenterologist, let me set the record straight.

First, the calming part: no food has been confirmed as the source — investigators are looking hardest at salad greens, but nothing’s confirmed. Swearing off all fresh produce does more harm than good. Most healthy people recover on their own, though it can linger for weeks and even relapse; treatment mainly shortens it and heads off relapse.

Now the myths. Oregano oil, grapefruit seed extract, and “parasite cleanses” have no reliable human evidence against this parasite. There’s no supplement shortcut. Washing helps and is worth doing, but no rinse — plain, vinegar, ozone, or peroxide — completely removes cyclospora, because it clings and resists sanitizing. Freezing lowers the load but doesn’t reliably kill it either. Thorough cooking (~158°F) is the safest.

The question I got most: what if you’re allergic to Bactrim? You’re not stuck. Nitazoxanide (Alinia, 500 mg twice daily for 7 days) is the alternative typically used for sulfa-allergic patients —though it’s a decision to make with your doctor.

Depression isn’t just in your head. A Harvard team identified one of the molecular pathways linking what’s happening in your gut to what’s happening in your brain.

The bacterium is Morganella morganii. Previous research had linked it to major depressive disorder. This new paper shows the mechanism: when M. morganii encounters an industrial pollutant called diethanolamine (DEA) — found in many everyday consumer products — it produces an altered fat molecule that activates the immune system through TLR2/TLR1 receptors and triggers the release of IL-6, one of the most-studied inflammatory cytokines linked to depression.

The chain: pollutant meets gut bacterium → molecule gets twisted → inflammation gets triggered. And inflammation has long been linked to mood.

Important: this is a mechanism study, not a clinical trial. It doesn’t prove that any individual person’s depression is caused by DEA exposure. What it does is explain, at a chemical level, how a gut microbe can influence brain health — making the gut-brain inflammation story more concrete than it’s ever been.

We act as if the body is compartmentalized. This is further proof that it’s all connected — gut, immune system, brain. Inflammation has a pattern. And it shows up in places we don’t expect.

caption:
If your gut microbes could talk, they would not thank you for a sardine fast.

Sardines are a healthy food when eaten as part of a balanced diet. They are rich in omega-3 fatty acids, high in protein, and packed with important nutrients.

But sardines contain zero dietary fibre, and your gut microbes rely on fibre from plants to survive and function. Without it, they have nothing to feed on and ferment. Even over a short period, removing fibre and plant diversity can disrupt the microbiome, which plays a central role in metabolic health.

This is why @theguthealthmd and I do not recommend single-food “fasts”. Your gut thrives on diversity, not restriction.
You may see short-term weight loss, but this is largely water loss and reduced calorie intake. It is not a sustainable or meaningful improvement in health.

There are other concerns too. High sodium intake from multiple tins a day, and the lack of balance you get from cutting out whole food groups.

If you want the benefits of sardines, the answer is much simpler. Eat them regularly as part of a varied, plant-rich diet.

Have you seen other diet trends like this doing the rounds? Let us know in the comments and we’ll take a look at the evidence.

caption:
PCOS just got a new name — PMOS, or Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome — and it’s the biggest change to a women’s health diagnosis in a generation.

170 million women worldwide are affected. Up to 70% are undiagnosed. This is a common but historically neglected condition, and one of the reasons it’s been neglected is the name.

For decades, PCOS has been treated as a gynecological problem. The Lancet consensus this week formally acknowledges what the research has been saying for years: this is a multisystem condition driven by insulin, androgens, and hormonal disturbances. Downstream, women with this diagnosis face higher rates of diabetes, fatty liver disease, cardiovascular disease, depression, and even skin and hair changes. All driven by the same upstream biology.

We act as if the body is compartmentalized. This is further proof that it’s all connected — ovaries, liver, skin, gut, inflammation. It’s not just an ovary problem.

If this sounds familiar, it’s because we did the same thing with fatty liver disease in 2023 — renaming NAFLD to MASLD to acknowledge the metabolic root. In fact, the PMOS consensus paper literally lists MASLD as one of the conditions PMOS shows up as. Same biology. Same nomenclature shift.

If you have this diagnosis, your symptoms are real. The condition is real. What’s changing is how we describe it, and that change opens up more useful ways to treat it. The question stops being “what’s wrong with my ovaries” and starts being “what’s happening with my insulin, my inflammation, and my gut?”

We’re walking through exactly that in my free workshop on Tuesday, May 26. Comment WORKSHOP below and I’ll send you the link.

Here's the exercise prescription I give every patient: minimum of 250 minutes a week. That's about 35 minutes a day. Here's how it breaks down and why.

~150 min/week of moderate cardio. This is the threshold where the data consistently shows lower cardiovascular disease risk (Piercy 2018; Bull/WHO 2020). It's not a magic cliff. Benefit starts below it, but it's the target worth aiming for.

~100 min/week of resistance training. Strength work is what packs the punch for lowering all-cause mortality and blood pressure. Mortality benefit shows up around 60 min/week (Shailendra 2022); I prescribe a bit more to also cover strength, function, and BP.

And if you're a woman, lift. Women tend to get equal or greater longevity benefit at the same, or even lower activity dose than men (Ji 2024, JACC; He 2025, NHANES), and resistance training is linked to lower hypertension risk specifically in women (Park & Park 2024).

So when a patient tells me they've got ~35 minutes a day, I tell them to split it: ~20 minutes of cardio, ~15 minutes of strength. That's the whole prescription. Most of the benefit comes from simply going from doing nothing to doing something.

Educational content, not individual medical advice. Talk to your clinician before starting a new program.

The headline: the most physically active quartile had 28% lower odds of IBS than the least active quartile (very active minutes, OR 0.72, p<0.001). Daily steps tracked the same direction (OR 0.82, p=0.028). And the highest-sedentary quartile had 24% higher odds (OR 1.24, p=0.007).

This is cross-sectional data. We can’t say walking prevents IBS from this study alone. But across 44,000 people, across four different objective movement metrics, the picture pointed in the same direction. More movement, less IBS. More sitting, more IBS. And the strongest effect — by a wide margin — was tied to very active minutes, the brisk and intentional kind of movement.

I’ve cared for thousands of patients with IBS over the years. One of the hardest conversations has always been telling someone to stay active without much hard data behind it. That conversation just got easier. This is the lever you can pull yourself — before the next prescription, before the next test.

This study is the case for what we’re doing together in May. The Gut Health Collective’s monthly challenge for May 2026 is The Walking Challenge — a four-week progression I designed to take you from sedentary to a 7,000-step brisk-walking habit one week at a time. Week 1 is a single 10-minute walk after a meal. Week 2 builds to 4,000 steps a day. Week 3 lands at 7,000. Week 4 keeps the count and adds the brisk pace this study highlighted.

You don’t need a gym. You don’t need expensive devices. You need shoes you can walk in, thirty minutes most days, and a community walking alongside you.

Featured Study: Loesch J et al. Am J Gastroenterol, 2026. PMID 42043274.

Perimenopause raises psychological symptom burden 52%. And it’s not what you think.

A new peer-reviewed study of 7,975 women across 20 countries measured it on the Menopause Rating Scale: 7.3 in perimenopause versus 4.8 in premenopause. We assume that load is anxiety and depression. It isn’t. The single largest jump was exhaustion, up 56%, followed by irritability. Depressive mood and anxiety rose too, but they were the smallest movers, not the headline.

And this is the part most coverage skips: the increase held after adjusting for age, education, income, ethnicity, BMI, smoking, alcohol, and an existing diagnosis of anxiety or depression. Something in the transition itself is driving it. The authors point to variability in estradiol and low progesterone, alongside psychosocial factors.

Clinical takeaway: perimenopausal exhaustion is not a productivity problem or a character flaw. It is a hormonal signal, and it is measurable. If you are wiped out, foggy, and forgetting words, that is not you failing. That is data.

Save this and send it to a woman who has been told it is just stress.

Source: Cunningham AC, Hedges MS, Hewings-Martin Y, Castaneda R, Karam J, Zhaunova L, Faubion SS, Shufelt CL. Psychological symptoms during perimenopause: a global perspective. Menopause. 2026;34(6). doi:10.1097/GME.0000000000002872

caption:
A randomized trial just measured something I never thought we’d be able to measure: the structure of a baby’s brain, in utero, by what the mother ate.
 
The IMPACT BCN trial randomized 1,221 pregnant women in Barcelona into three arms — Mediterranean diet, stress reduction, or usual care. A subset of 124 had MRIs late in the third trimester. The babies in the Mediterranean-diet arm had a measurably deeper right insula (P=0.03), a deeper left insula (P=0.01), and a longer corpus callosum (P<0.01) compared with the babies in the usual-care arm. The stress-reduction arm also showed a deeper left insula vs usual care (P=0.04) — same direction, smaller effect.
 
The Mediterranean-diet arm wasn’t a vague “eat Mediterranean” instruction. Participants got monthly counseling plus free olive oil and walnuts. The broader pattern — vegetables, fruit, legumes, fish, whole grains — was taught, not provided. A real protocol, not a label.
 
The effect sizes were real, but small. We don’t yet know what those structural differences mean for these kids at age five or fifteen. But they were detectable in utero, on MRI, from a dietary pattern. That alone is remarkable.
 
This is the kind of finding that strengthens the “diet quality matters” frame at the most consequential life stage of all. The Mediterranean pattern is one of the most well-studied templates in human nutrition, which is why it was heavily featured in my new book Plant Powered Plus. And now we see its effects during pregnancy.
 
Something that struck me about the design: the intervention didn’t start until mid-pregnancy. What if it started earlier? What if it started before pregnancy? Even a mid-pregnancy diet change is impactful — love that. But I’d encourage starting as early as possible. Even today. Why not?
 
If you’re pregnant or trying to be, the food choice you’re making is doing more work than you may realize.
 
Featured Study: Nakaki A et al. Effects of Mediterranean diet and stress-reduction interventions during pregnancy on fetal brain development detected using magnetic resonance imaging. Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology, 2026. PMID 41999106. DOI: 10.1002/uog.70214

Perimenopause raises psychological symptom burden 52%. And it’s not what you think.

A new peer-reviewed study of 7,975 women across 20 countries measured it on the Menopause Rating Scale: 7.3 in perimenopause versus 4.8 in premenopause. We assume that load is anxiety and depression. It isn’t. The single largest jump was exhaustion, up 56%, followed by irritability. Depressive mood and anxiety rose too, but they were the smallest movers, not the headline.

And this is the part most coverage skips: the increase held after adjusting for age, education, income, ethnicity, BMI, smoking, alcohol, and an existing diagnosis of anxiety or depression. Something in the transition itself is driving it. The authors point to variability in estradiol and low progesterone, alongside psychosocial factors.

Clinical takeaway: perimenopausal exhaustion is not a productivity problem or a character flaw. It is a hormonal signal, and it is measurable. If you are wiped out, foggy, and forgetting words, that is not you failing. That is data.

Save this and send it to a woman who has been told it is just stress.

caption:
A new study in Nature Medicine (published last week) just answered something I get asked constantly: does cutting back on plastic actually change anything in your body, and how fast can it happen?

The setup was simple. Researchers took 60 healthy adults and split them into five groups for 7 days. Some changed only their food. Some changed their kitchenware too. One group only swapped their personal-care products. One group did nothing — they were the comparison.

In one week, BPA dropped 60 percent in the group that changed both food and kitchenware. Two related plastic chemicals (called phthalates — they’re what makes plastic soft and flexible) dropped 44 and 53 percent. The personal-care group still dropped one of the chemicals by 35 percent without changing a single food item.

Here’s the interesting part. The food group didn’t eat less produce. They were eating the same amount of fruits and vegetables. They just changed how it was packaged and they cut canned foods for the week. And the plastic chemicals in their bodies still fell by more than half. The packaging is the opportunity, the produce needs to stay.

One honest note. Not every plastic chemical responded. There’s a specific one called DEHP that didn’t drop in seven days. The researchers think it gets stored in fat tissue, and that household dust and indoor air contribute as much as food does. We need longer studies. But at least for this one, 7 days of less plastic in the diet wasn’t enough.

None of us has been immune to plastic. This isn’t about what you should have done. It’s about what you can do next. Pick one swap this week. That’s it.

Save this for grocery day. And send this to the one person in your life who keeps asking ‘is BPA actually a real thing?’

Featured Study: Harray AJ, Lucas AD, Herrmann SE, et al. Nature Medicine 2026. PMID 42014506. DOI 10.1038/s41591-026-04324-7.

Swap plastic cutting boards, plastic wrap, and worn utensils for wood, glass, stainless steel, or silicone.
	
6.	Avoid hot food and drinks in plastic
Use ceramic, glass, or stainless steel for hot foods and hot liquids instead of plastic.

One of the biggest mysteries in women's health is hiding in plain sight. Our ovaries age at least twice as fast as the rest of our bodies. 

✨Comment POD for the link to the full episode of unPAUSED with Dr. Jennifer Garrison, PhD. 

That isn't just about fertility. Ovaries produce hormones that influence nearly every organ system, including the brain, heart, bones, muscles, metabolism, and immune system. When ovarian function declines decades before many other organs, it may help explain why women's health changes so dramatically during and after menopause.

The question is...why?
As Jennifer Garrison, PhD, explains, scientists still don't have the answer.

Unlike the male reproductive system, which tends to age alongside the rest of the body, ovarian function declines much earlier. Understanding why that happens could unlock new ways to improve health span, delay disease, and change how we think about aging in women.

This is exactly why women's health research deserves more attention and more investment. The answers won't just improve menopause care. They could transform how we prevent disease across a woman's lifetime.

caption:
Can muscle loss begin in perimenopause, before your final period? Research suggests it can. Changes in muscle mass, strength, power, and motor function may already be underway during the menopause transition.
 
This matters because muscle is not only about size. Lower-body strength and power help determine whether you can catch yourself, rise from a chair, carry what you need, and remain independent.

Most routine care is designed to find disease. It is not designed to notice the early loss of strength that can quietly change how you move through the world. Your bloodwork can look reassuring while the stairs feel steeper, the groceries feel heavier, and getting off the floor takes more effort than it used to.
 
We still do not have a trial proving that starting resistance training in perimenopause produces better outcomes than starting later. But waiting for obvious weakness makes little sense when we already know muscle changes may begin during the transition.
 
Do not wait for weakness to become the evidence. The earlier you pay attention to strength, the more of it you may have to carry forward.
 
Sources: Wright et al., Climacteric, 2024; Sipilä et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle, 2020; Park et al., J Appl Physiol, 2020; Pesonen et al., BMC Women’s Health, 2021; Pyle, Physiol Genomics, 2026; da Silva Rodrigues et al., Physiol Genomics, 2026.

Hair loss in midlife is rarely caused by just one thing.

Your hair follicles depend on hormones, nutrients, thyroid function, sleep, and overall health to stay in their normal growth cycle. When one or more of those systems is disrupted, shedding and thinning can follow.

Some of the most common contributors include:
• Female pattern hair loss
• Telogen effluvium
• Iron deficiency
• Thyroid dysfunction
• Other nutrient deficiencies and certain medications

The good news? Many causes of hair loss can be evaluated and, in some cases, treated once you know what's behind it.

caption:
If you keep losing words, forgetting why you walked into a room, or struggling to focus during perimenopause, there may be more going on than stress.
 
A new 12-month study followed 150 perimenopausal women and 80 premenopausal controls, tracking estradiol, inflammation, BDNF, memory, and brain changes. Declining estradiol was linked with shifts in markers tied to neural health, higher inflammation, lower memory performance, and reduced hippocampal volume.
 
The study cannot prove that estradiol caused each change, but it does strengthen the case for taking perimenopause brain fog seriously. Sleep, mood, medications, thyroid function, iron levels, ADHD, and other health factors can also play a role. Bring cognitive symptoms into the conversation with your clinician.
 
Brain fog during perimenopause deserves a real evaluation.
 
Source: Liu, Huang & Zeng, “Estradiol reduction during perimenopause is associated with lower BDNF, elevated inflammation, hippocampal loss, and cognitive decline,” Experimental Gerontology, 2026.

caption:
Vaginal estrogen may be the most underused sepsis-and-death-prevention tool we have. I am not being dramatic.

A new study in Urology analyzed Epic Cosmos electronic health records from 1,891,956 women with recurrent UTIs. Women prescribed vaginal estrogen had markedly lower rates of:
→ Sepsis (odds 0.22 to 0.46) 
→ Hospitalization (odds 0.31 to 0.62) 
→ Death (odds 0.20 to 0.38, roughly 60 to 80 percent lower)

And it held across every age group, 20 to 99. The mortality gap is hard to look away from. At ages 55 to 69: 1.5 percent died with vaginal estrogen versus 7.3 percent without.

Now the honesty, because it matters. This is observational. The authors name the biggest limitation themselves: healthy-prescriber bias. Women who get this prescription often have clinicians who provide better care across the board, so the prescription may mark good care as much as cause good outcomes. This does not prove vaginal estrogen prevents death.

But the signal is enormous and consistent, and it points at a system failure, not a patient one. Only about 5 percent of women received vaginal estrogen within two months of diagnosis. Only about 1 in 4 were ever prescribed it at all. A guideline-recommended, low-cost, low-risk therapy, reaching a fraction of the women it is written for.

The AUA/CUA/SUFU Recurrent UTI Guideline (2025) is explicit: clinicians should recommend vaginal estrogen to reduce the risk of future UTIs if there is no contraindication (Grade B). And in November 2025, the FDA removed the boxed warning on low-dose vaginal estrogen.

So if you get repeat UTIs, take one question to your doctor: why am I not a candidate?

Grateful to Dr. Elise De (@elisede123) and her team at Albany Med for this work, and to Dr. Rachel Rubin (@drrachelrubin) for her relentless work getting vaginal estrogen the attention it deserves.

Source: LaClair J, Visingardi J, Wells B, Feustel P, Deckert J, De EJB. Vaginal Estrogen Prescription is Associated with Reduced Risk of Serious Adverse Outcomes in Women of All Age Groups with Recurrent Urinary Tract Infection: An Epic Cosmos Database Analysis. Urology, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.urology.2026.06.004

caption:
Heavy bleeding in perimenopause deserves more than “your hormones are changing.”
 
Adenomyosis is one possible explanation, and many women do not hear the word until they are diagnosed. Its symptoms can overlap with fibroids, endometriosis, and the changing cycles of perimenopause, making it harder to understand what is actually causing the bleeding or pain. Your uterine history may matter, too. If your symptoms changed after a C-section, D&C, fibroid removal, or another uterine procedure, say so. That timing may help explain what is happening.
 
The same goes for bleeding that begins after starting or changing menopausal hormone therapy. It deserves a careful evaluation that looks at the timing, the hormone regimen, progestogen protection, and possible uterine causes. Heavy bleeding is not something you should be expected to endure. You deserve answers and treatment options.

I want you to sit with that number. One hundred grams of fiber a day. That’s not a typo.

Anthropological research on hunter-gatherer populations and studies of traditional societies still eating ancestral diets have found fiber intakes ranging from 50 to over 150 grams daily— from an enormous variety of plant sources including tubers, legumes, wild fruits, seeds, and fibrous vegetables.

Our gut microbiome evolved in that context. The bacterial populations that colonize our colon, the enzymes they produce, the metabolic pathways they run— all of it developed under conditions of fiber abundance and diversity. Then in a geologic instant, we shifted to a processed food diet delivering 15 grams from a handful of sources. The microbiome hasn’t had time to adapt. And we’re seeing the consequences: declining microbial diversity across industrialized populations, rising rates of colorectal cancer, metabolic disease, and inflammatory conditions— all with established connections to microbiome disruption.

The good news: the microbiome is responsive. You don’t have to reach 100 grams. Moving from 15 toward 30, 40, 50— from more diverse sources— produces measurable changes in bacterial composition and inflammatory markers.

Start where you are and move the number up.

caption:
Five things I added to my own routine that the data says reduce inflammation. Each takes five minutes or less. None of them is a detox.

Pick the ones that fit your life. You have choices.

Fiber → most people get about 15g a day. The target is closer to 30. A randomized crossover trial showed CRP reductions of 13.7–18.1% when participants moved from baseline (~12g/day) to 30g/day. (PMID 17353499)

Fermented foods → Stanford ran a 10-week intervention with kimchi, kefir, yogurt, and sauerkraut. The fermented food arm saw decreased inflammatory markers and increased microbiome diversity. (PMID 34256014).

Walnuts → both plant omega-3 (ALA) and polyphenols in one food. The 2-year Walnuts and Healthy Aging trial measured a clear shift toward anti-inflammatory lipid biomarkers in daily walnut eaters versus controls. (PMID 38081585).

Light walking after meals → In a meta-analysis of 7 trials, even brief light walking after meals significantly reduces the after meal blood glucose spike. (PMID 35147898)

Sleep window → consistency matters just as much as the absolute number of hours. Irregular sleep timing elevates inflammatory markers even when total hours look adequate. (PMID 31289370).

An important point for the research nerds: these are directional, not the exact doses the studies measured. 30g of fiber, 10 weeks of high-dose daily fermented foods, 2 years of daily walnuts — those are the studied amounts. What I’m proposing is the on-ramp that starts the process of moving towards these goals. In practice, once you start moving in a direction, it gets easier to keep moving. Over time, you reach the doses that were actually validated.

Five weird signs your gut is actually healthy

1. Your stomach growls and rumbles (even loudly!).
It’s basically your gut’s cleaning cycle. Those sounds happen when waves of contractions move gas, fluid, and leftover food through your intestines between meals. This process—called the migrating motor complex—helps sweep bacteria and debris through the small intestine and eventually to the colon.

2. You fart all the time.
Your gut bacteria are extracting antioxidants from your food, fermenting fiber, producing anti-inflammatory compounds, and producing gas as a byproduct. Most healthy people pass gas around 10–20 times per day, and it’s often a sign your microbiome is actively doing its job.

3. You poop shortly after eating or when you’re excited.
This is the gastrocolic reflex. When your stomach stretches from a meal—or when your body is stimulated by things like excitement—it signals the colon to contract and move stool along. Your body is essentially making room for incoming food.

4. You have ghost poop.
That’s when you poop and there’s almost nothing to wipe. Well-formed stool that passes easily and leaves minimal residue is often a sign of good fiber intake, hydration, and balanced gut bacteria.

5. You poop more than once a day.
A lot of people think once per day is the rule, but pooping up to about 3 times per day can be normal. The key is that the stool should be formed and easy to pass. Frequent watery stools or diarrhea would be abnormal.
